newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans collapse, longs bail out of July.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans collapse, longs bail out of July.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures collapsed on Tuesday, led by July as concerns of tight nearby supplies eased, pit sources said.

"The purported squeeze in the July was thwarted," said John Kleist, analyst with Sagamore Partners. "What stopped it was the realization that you can increase supplies by switching old crop sales to new crop, by cancelling old crop sales, by getting early (harvested) beans out of the South, and by importing beans from Brazil."
The July contract fell to its lowest level since January, gutted by heavy fund, commission house and local selling.

The spot month had been propped up by concerns of tight supplies and the lack of deliverable stocks. Rumors have been swirling for weeks that a commercial firm would deliver soybeans but none have been posted.
New crop November continued to reel from Monday's U.S. Agriculture Department's 1997 soybean acreage forecast.
November fell 58 cents a bushel in two days after USDA put plantings at 70.85 million acres, the third largest planted area on record and well above trade expectations.
Soybeans ended 39 to 15 cents per bushel lower with July down 39 at $7.32 and November off 28 at $5.89-1/2.

Perceptions of ideal growing weather compounded weakness in new crop November. USDA's weekly crop update released Monday afternoon showed 65 percent of the soybean crop was in good to excellent shape, up from 61 percent the previous week.
Some analysts predicted 1997 U.S. soybean output at a record 2.8 billion bushels.
Contract lows were notched in the September, November, January, March, May and July 1998 contracts.
The July/November spread traded firm for much of the session but fell apart in the waning minutes of trade to close down 11 cents a bushel at $1.42-1/2, premium July.
July traded as low as $7.13 in late dealings, down 58 cents. Pit sources said Griffin Trading, Prudential Securities and Refco Inc were aggressive sellers late.
Floor sources said a small-lot sale at $7.23 triggered large sell stops which took the market down to $7.13. They said a fund bought one million bushels on the close which triggered a late recovery.
On the day, Griffin Trading sold at least 14 million bushels, including nine million bushels November. Refco Inc sold at least 10 million bushles and Prudential Securities sold at least nine million.
FIMAT Futures bought at least 16 million bushels on the day while Merrill Lynch bought 7.5 million November.
In options trade, FIMAT bought 1,500 November $7.00 calls and sold 1,500 November $6.50 calls at seven to 6-1/4 cents.
Volatility in the August was pegged at 26 percent and November was at 20 percent.
Soybean futures volume was estimated at 100,000 contracts, compared with Monday's actual volume of 64,090 contracts.
